title: Objects and Classes
summary: The substrate under the four OOP pillars: what a class and object actually are, identity vs equality, where state lives, and how `this`/`self` binds a method to its object.

slides.markdown:
A **class** is a blueprint: it describes what data an object holds and what it can do, but by itself it computes nothing. An **object** is one instantiation of that blueprint — a real chunk of memory with its own state, sitting at its own address.

This topic covers the substrate under the four OOP pillars: identity vs equality, where state actually lives, how a method finds "its" object, and the pitfalls that come from getting any of that wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: What a class actually is: a blueprint, not a template you copy
slides.markdown:
A **class** is a compiled description — field names, types, and method bodies — not a stamped-out copy of anything. Defining `class Car { String make; void drive() {} }` allocates zero memory for cars; it just tells the runtime what a `Car` *would* look like if one existed.

Memory only gets allocated when you call `new Car()` — that's when an **object** is born, with its own copy of the instance fields. A hundred `Car` objects share one class definition (one copy of the compiled method) but each carries its own `make`.

The interview trap: confusing "class" with "instance" when asked to explain memory layout — the class lives once, in the method area/metaspace; objects live per-instance, on the heap.

An **object** bundles three things that only make sense together: **state** (the current values of its fields), **identity** (a distinct existence in memory, even if two objects hold identical state), and **behavior** (the methods it can invoke, which read and mutate that state).

Create two `Car` objects with the same make and model — `new Car("Honda", "Civic")` twice — and you get two objects with identical state but different identity: they live at different addresses, changing one's mileage doesn't touch the other, and `car1 == car2` is false even though they "look" the same.

Behavior is what ties state to identity: `car1.drive()` only ever mutates `car1`'s own fields, never `car2`'s — that's what "its own object" means in practice.

A **constructor** is the method that runs exactly once, at the moment an object is created, to get it into a valid starting state — that's its whole job, not general-purpose logic that happens to run early.

Initialization order inside a single class is stricter than most people assume: fields first get their declared or default values (`0`, `null`, `false`), *then* the constructor body runs and can overwrite them. So `class Counter { int count = 10; Counter() { count = 20; } }` ends with `count == 20` — the field initializer runs first, then the constructor body wins.

The practical rule: never leave an object able to exist in an invalid state — if a field is required, take it as a constructor parameter, don't default it and hope someone sets it later.

Every instance method secretly receives one extra, invisible parameter: a reference to the object it was called on — `this` in Java/C++/JavaScript, `self` in Python (there it's explicit, not hidden). Write `car.drive()` and the runtime effectively calls `drive(car)`; inside the method, `this`/`self` *is* that `car`.

That's how `this.mileage += distance;` knows *which* object's mileage to update when a thousand `Car` objects all share the same compiled `drive` method — there's one method body, but `this` binds it to a specific object on each call.

It also explains a common error: calling an instance method with no instance in scope (a static context) fails, because there's no object left to bind `this` to.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: object references vs values in memory
slides.markdown:
A variable holding an object doesn't hold the object itself — it holds a **reference** (effectively an address) pointing at the object's data on the heap. Assign `Car a = b;` and you now have two references pointing at the *same* object: mutating through `a` is visible through `b`, because there's only one `Car` in memory.

Contrast that with a **value** (a primitive `int`, or a value type in some languages): `int x = y;` copies the number itself — there's nothing shared to mutate.

![Two references a and b pointing to the same Car object versus two independent int values each holding their own copy of 5](assets/reference-vs-value.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: Equality vs identity: `==` vs `.equals()`, value vs reference comparison
slides.markdown:
**Identity** asks "are these the exact same object in memory?" **Equality** asks "do these objects represent the same value?" Two different `Point(1,2)` objects can be equal without being identical.

| | Identity | Equality |
|---|---|---|
| Java | `==` on objects | `.equals()` (override it yourself) |
| Python | `is` | `==` (calls `__eq__`) |
| C++ | pointer/reference compare | `operator==` overload |
| Default behavior | always identity-based | falls back to identity if unoverridden |

**How to decide:** use identity when you need to know if two variables point at the literal same object (singleton checks, caching); use equality — and override it deliberately — whenever "same value" is what your domain actually cares about, like comparing two `Money` amounts.

slides.sectionTitle: Static vs instance members: what belongs to the class vs the object
slides.markdown:
An **instance member** (field or method) belongs to one object — each `Car` has its own `mileage`. A **static member** belongs to the class itself — there's exactly one copy, shared by every instance and reachable without creating any object at all (`Car.numberOfCarsCreated`).

The classic legitimate use: a counter tracking how many objects have been created, incremented inside the constructor — `static int count; Car() { count++; }`. Every `Car` shares that single `count`, which is exactly the point.

The classic misuse: reaching for `static` to avoid passing an object around, which quietly turns per-object data into shared global state — see the next slide's pitfall for where that breaks.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a minimal class showing state, constructor, and a method
Pitfall: mutable default/static state accidentally shared across instances
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll give this field a sensible default at the class level so every object starts with an empty list — `static List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();`."

**Why it's wrong:** `static` means one shared list across *every* instance, not a fresh list per object. Add a tag through one `Car` and every other `Car` sees it too — a bug that often surfaces only after hundreds of objects exist and someone notices state leaking between unrelated instances.

**Correct model:** default values that should be per-object belong on an **instance** field, initialized in the constructor (`this.tags = new ArrayList<>();`) or as a non-static field initializer — one fresh list per object, every time. Reserve `static` for state that is genuinely meant to be shared, like a class-wide counter.
